questions.question_text: What must all DC real estate advertising include?
distractors: The salesperson's license number
The property's assessed value
The listing price in bold text
questions.explanation: DCMR 17-2615 requires all advertising to be in the name of the firm, with the firm's licensed name displayed clearly and legibly, and all advertising must be under the direct supervision of the principal or supervising broker. A salesperson's name may also appear.

questions.question_text: A DC salesperson posts a property listing on social media using only their personal name, without mentioning their broker. Is this permitted?
questions.correct_answer: No, all advertising must be in the firm's name
distractors: Yes, social media is exempt from ad rules
Yes, if the post is not a paid advertisement
Only if the property is their own listing
questions.explanation: DC advertising rules apply to all media, including social media. DCMR 17-2615 requires every advertisement to be in the name of the firm, with the firm's licensed name displayed clearly and legibly. Posting without firm identification is a blind ad, which is prohibited.

questions.question_text: What is a 'blind ad' in DC real estate?
distractors: An ad that conceals the property address
An ad targeted to a specific demographic
An ad placed by an unlicensed person
questions.explanation: A blind ad is one that does not identify the licensed firm, making it appear as though the salesperson or property owner is acting independently. DCMR 17-2615 requires the firm's licensed name on all advertising, so blind ads are prohibited in DC.

questions.question_text: A DC licensee writes an ad saying 'Perfect home in a quiet, family-friendly neighborhood.' Under DC law, what concern does this raise?
questions.correct_answer: Potential fair housing violation in advertising
distractors: Misleading property condition claims
Failure to include the listing price
Using subjective terms in advertising
questions.explanation: The phrase 'family-friendly' could be interpreted as indicating a preference for families, potentially violating fair housing laws. DC advertising must comply with both DCHRA and federal fair housing requirements.

questions.question_text: Which media are covered by DC's real estate advertising rules?
questions.correct_answer: All media including print, online, and signage
distractors: Only print media and yard signs
Only paid advertisements in publications
Only MLS listings and brokerage websites
questions.explanation: DC advertising rules apply to all media: print, online, social media, signage, and any other form of communication. The firm's licensed name must appear in every advertisement regardless of format, and online ads must contain or link to the required disclosure.

questions.question_text: How long must a DC licensee keep the brokerage-relationship disclosure notices for a transaction?
questions.correct_answer: 3 years from the fully executed purchase contract
distractors: 1 year from the transaction date
5 years from the date of first contact
7 years as required by federal law
questions.explanation: DCMR 17-2613.3 and D.C. Code § 47-2853.196(f) require the licensee to keep copies of the disclosure notices relating to a fully executed purchase contract for 3 years. DC sets no separate retention period for listing files or trust-account records, although escrow records must be kept accurate and available to the Board.

questions.question_text: Which of the following documents must a DC broker retain as part of their transaction records?
distractors: Only the final closing statement
Only documents the client requests
Only documents filed with DLCP
questions.explanation: Brokers must retain all transaction documents including listing agreements, purchase contracts, trust account records, correspondence, and disclosures for the full 3-year retention period.

questions.question_text: A transaction closes in January 2025. The broker's records related to this transaction must be kept until at least:
distractors: January 2026
January 2030
January 2032
questions.explanation: DC's 3-year retention runs from the fully executed purchase contract, which is signed before closing. Disclosure records for a transaction that closed in January 2025 are therefore safely retained through at least January 2028.

questions.question_text: A DC consumer refuses to sign the agency disclosure the licensee provides. What must the licensee do?
questions.correct_answer: Note the date of the refusal and the reason given
distractors: Stop working with the consumer until they sign
File a report with DLCP within 10 days
Have a witness sign the disclosure instead
questions.explanation: DCMR 17-2613 requires the licensee to ask the consumer to sign, date and return a copy of the disclosure. If the consumer declines, the licensee documents the date of the refusal and the reason the consumer gave on the disclosure notice itself. A refusal to sign does not stop the licensee from providing services.

questions.question_text: Which records are included in the DC broker's retention obligation?
questions.correct_answer: Disclosure notices tied to a ratified purchase contract
distractors: Only the settlement statement and deed
Only DLCP-required filing documents
Every email exchanged with a client, for 7 years
questions.explanation: DC's express retention rule (DCMR 17-2613.3) covers copies of the brokerage-relationship disclosure notices relating to a fully executed purchase contract, kept for 3 years. Brokers also have a continuing duty to maintain accurate escrow and client accounting records available for inspection, but DC sets no fixed term for those.

questions.question_text: A DC salesperson advertises listings by email and on a personal website. What do DC's advertising rules require?
questions.correct_answer: The required disclosure must appear on the page and in the email
distractors: Online advertising is exempt from DC disclosure rules
Only the brokerage's own website must carry a disclosure
A disclosure is required only for paid online ads
questions.explanation: DCMR 17-2615 applies to online advertising as well as print. Web pages must contain the disclosure or link to it, email and newsgroup postings must carry it at the beginning or end of the message, chat sessions require it before services are offered, and banner or pop-up ads must contain or link to it. Licensees may not use unsolicited commercial email.

questions.question_text: What does E&O insurance protect a DC licensee against?
questions.correct_answer: Claims of professional negligence or mistakes
distractors: Physical injury to clients at showings
Property damage during open houses
Loss of the broker's personal property
questions.explanation: E&O insurance covers claims arising from professional negligence, errors or omissions in real estate practice. It does not cover physical injuries (that is general liability) or personal property loss. DC does not require licensees to carry E&O - unlike the 14 states that do - but many brokerages require it of their agents.

questions.question_text: A DC licensee fails to disclose a known zoning violation, and the buyer sues for damages. Which insurance would cover this claim?
distractors: The broker's general liability policy
The seller's homeowner's insurance
The title insurance policy
questions.explanation: Failing to disclose a known zoning violation is a professional error or omission, which is exactly what E&O insurance is designed to cover. E&O is optional in DC rather than a licensing requirement, so whether coverage exists depends on the brokerage's own policy.

questions.question_text: Under DC's Code of Ethics, licensees must treat all parties to a transaction with which standard?
distractors: Equal fiduciary obligation to all parties
Preferential treatment to their own client
Strict neutrality without any advice
questions.explanation: DC's professional standards require honesty and fairness to all parties. While agents owe fiduciary duties to their clients, they must still be honest and fair with all other parties in the transaction.

questions.question_text: How must a DC licensee maintain their professional competence throughout their career?
distractors: By retaking the licensing exam every 5 years
Through annual peer review evaluations
By attending Commission meetings monthly
questions.explanation: DC requires ongoing professional competence through the 15-hour CE requirement each renewal cycle. This ensures licensees stay current on laws, ethics, fair housing, and practice standards.
